description: Retrieval-only development fixture: 20 pre-segmented passages and 60 questions. Not real manuals, a held-out test set, or operating instructions.
provenance: AI-authored synthetic passages, questions, and relevance labels; no real equipment incidents or manufacturer claims.

chunks.text: A centrifugal pump record links low discharge pressure to a blocked suction strainer, a partly closed inlet valve, or inadequate inlet pressure. The investigation compares suction pressure and delivered flow with the pump baseline. This entry concerns poor hydraulic output, not seal leakage or bearing heat.

The cavitation entry describes gravel-like rattling, fluctuating flow, and pitting near a centrifugal pump impeller. Vapor bubbles can form when inlet conditions are inadequate and collapse inside the pump. Suction conditions distinguish this hydraulic noise from the repetitive sound of a damaged rolling bearing.

A pump bearing-temperature trend rises while delivered flow stays stable. The maintenance record considers lubrication condition and shaft alignment. Housing temperature and vibration are compared with prior readings. This entry does not supply an operating temperature limit; limits must come from the equipment's approved documentation.

A wet trace around the pump shaft and liquid escaping near the seal housing point to the mechanical seal assembly. The record distinguishes shaft-seal leakage from a pipe flange leak. Inspection findings include seal-face condition and alignment; the entry is not a procedure for working on a running pump.

A rotary screw compressor has a low lubricating-oil pressure alarm despite normal delivery air pressure. The record compares oil level, lubricant pressure readings, and oil-filter condition. Lubrication pressure is a different circuit from the compressed-air outlet. Bypassing the alarm is not an acceptable diagnostic action.

A compressor discharge-air temperature trend increases when the cooler surface is fouled or cooling airflow is restricted. The record includes ambient temperature and fan observations. This thermal entry is separate from a low oil-pressure alarm and does not define a universal shutdown temperature.

Repeated short load-unload cycles are recorded on an air compressor when demand changes rapidly, a receiver is undersized, or the pressure-control band is unsuitable. The useful evidence is a timestamped pressure trace with loading states. This problem concerns cycling frequency rather than discharge-air temperature.

Water collected downstream of an air compressor is associated with condensate-drain or dryer performance. The record reviews drain observations, dew point, and dryer status. It distinguishes liquid water carryover from compressor lubricant pressure problems; the presence of water alone does not identify which component failed.

A motor overload trip coincides with sustained high current on all phases while driving a heavily loaded conveyor. Current history and mechanical load observations help distinguish excess demand from a supply imbalance. A trip label alone is not proof that the overload setting should be changed.

Unequal phase currents accompanied by unequal line voltages suggest a motor supply imbalance or connection issue. The diagnostic record compares all three phases rather than only the largest current value. This differs from roughly balanced high currents caused by excessive mechanical load.

A repeating rumble localised at a motor bearing is correlated with vibration and lubrication history. The record contrasts this rotating mechanical noise with a pump's gravel-like hydraulic noise. Supply-voltage measurements belong to a different diagnostic branch and do not directly confirm bearing damage.

A motor's insulation-resistance history changes after moisture exposure or storage in a damp environment. Qualified electrical assessment considers temperature, contamination, and earlier insulation measurements. This entry concerns winding insulation condition, not phase-current balance, and gives no procedure for testing energised equipment.

A conveyor belt migrates sideways and rubs one edge. The record links mistracking to pulley or idler alignment and uneven loading across the belt. Lateral position is the key observation. Tracking is different from a belt that stays centred but moves too slowly relative to its drive pulley.

The drive pulley rotates while the conveyor belt lags or stops intermittently, indicating relative slip. The record considers belt tension and contamination at the drive contact surface. Comparing pulley rotation with belt travel separates loss of traction from sideways belt tracking.

Material accumulates at a conveyor transfer chute and belt movement becomes obstructed. The record pairs blockage observations with drive-current history. This differs from a false photoeye indication when the transfer path is actually clear. Any physical inspection remains subject to the site's approved isolation procedure.

A conveyor photoelectric sensor reports an occupied path even when no item is present. The record considers a dirty lens, misalignment, and reflector condition. Comparing the indicated state with a clear physical path helps distinguish a false presence signal from an actual accumulation at the transfer chute.

A control valve remains stationary through small command changes and then jumps suddenly. The record calls this stick-slip behaviour and relates it to stem friction or packing condition. A stepped command-versus-motion trace is more informative here than a single final position reading.

A valve's position transmitter disagrees with an independently observed stem position even when the stem moves smoothly. The record concerns feedback calibration or linkage, not abrupt stick-slip motion. Comparing the command, actual movement, and reported position separates sensing error from mechanical friction.

A process filter shows increasing differential pressure at comparable flow as its element loads with retained material. Comparing pressures upstream and downstream distinguishes filter restriction from a change in pump inlet pressure. The record contains no universal replacement threshold for every filter design.

A pressure transmitter gradually diverges from a calibrated reference while the process appears stable. The record investigates zero shift and calibration history. It separates an instrument offset from a genuine pressure change confirmed by independent measurements. A single disagreeing reading is not sufficient proof of drift.

Outlet air pressure is normal; it is the lubricant pressure alarm that is active. Which entry applies?
The issue is poor liquid delivery pressure at a centrifugal pump, not lubricant pressure in an air machine.
The motor's currents are uneven between phases, rather than all being similarly high. Which record fits?
All motor phase currents are comparably high under mechanical load, not unbalanced. Which record fits?
The transfer chute is clear, but the conveyor presence detector still says occupied. Which record fits?
There is actual material blocking the conveyor transfer path, not just a false detector indication.
The valve moves smoothly but the position transmitter is wrong; there is no stick-slip jump.
The valve really sticks then jumps; the issue is not merely an incorrect position display.
Independent pressure references remain stable while one transmitter drifts. Which record fits?
Independent pressure measurements confirm growing loss across the process filter at similar flow, not just one drifting transmitter.
